title: A Shift then a Skip: Here's How One Teacher's Job Changed with a Simple Change in Thinking
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a reader-submitted story from Robert Macfadden, a veteran history teacher whose worst year of teaching -- marked by anxiety attacks, endless grading, and a school-shooting lockdown at a nearby campus -- became the catalyst for a single realization: no one but Robert himself had decided he had to grade everything. By cutting his grading load and concentrating his effort on assessments that actually moved student performance (turning around AP essays in a weekend instead of weeks), Robert's anxiety attacks stopped, his confidence returned, and he went on to take on new roles (PBIS coordinator, further coursework) from a place of surplus rather than depletion. Stuart uses the story to argue that Robert's original, harried state is the professional default for teachers, not an aberration, and that what changed his trajectory wasn't a new job, a new assignment, or an intervention from administration, but an internal shift in belief about what success required. The piece frames this as the pattern behind the blog's SKIP discipline within its life-stewardship framework: a tiny internal realization producing an outsized practical result.
points: Macfadden's turnaround came entirely from an internal belief shift -- "the only thing that said I had to grade endless papers and assignments was me" -- with no change in school, class assignment, or administrative support.

Reducing grading volume while increasing the meaning of what he did grade let him turn AP essays around in a weekend instead of weeks, directly improving both his anxiety and his students' performance feedback loop.

Stuart frames Macfadden's pre-realization exhaustion as the professional default for teachers, not a personal failing, positioning worsening teacher attrition as a predictable consequence of that default state.
The story illustrates the blog's recurring principle that tiny, internal shifts in what a teacher believes they "have to" do can produce outsized, durable changes in workload and wellbeing.
quotes: I was spending way too much time grading things my students were just cheating on, my lessons themselves had stagnated, and I was no longer receiving feedback from observers because I managed student behavior well.
I realized that the only thing that said I had to grade endless papers and assignments was me. I reduced my grading load while increasing the meaning that the things I did do with my student had.

Instead of taking weeks to grade SAQs and LEQs, I was giving them on Friday and handing them back graded on Monday. The anxiety attacks disappeared, and I had a newfound confidence in what I was doing in my classroom.

We're a set of professionals rife with anxiety, overwhelm, and a sense of stagnation. The default conditions of our work are either frenetic, unceasing attempts to manage impossible task sets OR frustrated resignation to the senseless chaos that is the modern education system's initiative/policy/program maelstrom.

Instead, what happened is that Robert broke through an inner obstacle: the belief that he had to grade everything. When he had to grade everything — when this is how he defined success — success became impossible, effort became meaningless, and the work lost its value.
Tiny change. Large result. What tiny changes might be whispering to you right now?
